checkpoint.question: What fundamental problem do Java Generic wildcards (? extends T, ? super T) solve in object-oriented type systems?
options: They overcome generic type invariance, allowing collections of subtypes or supertypes to be safely passed to reusable methods
They allow Java collections to dynamically resize at runtime
They enable primitive data types to be stored directly inside collections without boxing
They bypass compile-time type checking to permit arbitrary objects into lists
checkpoint.explanation: In Java, generics are invariant: List<Integer> is NOT a subtype of List<Number>, even though Integer extends Number. Wildcards introduce use-site covariance (? extends Number) and contravariance (? super Integer).

pages.title: 1. Prerequisite check
pages.content: Before starting **Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards**, recall the Java syntax and object/model concepts required for it. Write down what you already know, then identify one question you cannot yet answer confidently. The purpose of this step is to expose a missing prerequisite before new material is introduced.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 1. prerequisite check for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

checkpoint.question: Why does List<Number> list = new ArrayList<Integer>(); fail to compile, whereas Number[] array = new Integer[10]; compiles?
options: Java arrays are covariant (which can cause runtime ArrayStoreException), whereas Java generics are invariant to guarantee compile-time type safety
Integer does not inherit from Number in the generic type hierarchy
ArrayList does not implement the List interface
Generics only support primitive types
checkpoint.explanation: Java arrays are covariant, meaning Integer[] is a subtype of Number[] (checked at runtime). Generic types are invariant (List<Integer> is NOT a List<Number>) to prevent putting a Double into an integer list at compile time.

pages.title: 2. Build the concept
pages.content: Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards should be learned through a progression from terminology and mental model to tracing, implementation, and independent application. Start with the rule, then connect the rule to one small Java example. Avoid memorizing a code template before you can explain why each important line is present.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 2. build the concept for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

checkpoint.question: When a method accepts List<? extends Number> list, which operation is permitted by the Java compiler?
options: Number n = list.get(0); (reading elements as Number)
list.add(Integer.valueOf(10)); (adding an Integer)
list.add(Double.valueOf(3.14)); (adding a Double)
list.add(new Object()); (adding an Object)
checkpoint.explanation: An upper-bounded wildcard ? extends Number is read-only (producer): the compiler knows elements are at least Number, so reading as Number is safe. Adding is disallowed (except null) because the underlying list could be a List<Double>.

pages.title: 3. Build a mental model
pages.content: Imagine the runtime state while **Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards** executes. Identify the important actors, ownership, values, references, control flow, or exception paths. Explain the relationship in plain language before touching a full program.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 3. build a mental model for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

checkpoint.question: When a method accepts List<? super Integer> list, which element can safely be added to list?
options: list.add(Integer.valueOf(42));
list.add(new Object());
list.add(Double.valueOf(3.14));
list.add(new Number());
checkpoint.explanation: A lower-bounded wildcard ? super Integer is a consumer: the actual list is of Integer or a supertype (like Number or Object). Therefore, adding an Integer (or subtype) is always type-safe.

checkpoint.question: Which syntax correctly declares a generic method with multiple bounds requiring type parameter T to extend Comparable<T> and implement Serializable?
options: <T extends Comparable<T> & Serializable>
<T extends Comparable<T>, Serializable>
<T implements Comparable<T> & Serializable>
<T extends Comparable<T> | Serializable>
checkpoint.explanation: In Java generics, multiple bounds use the & operator (e.g., <T extends ClassA & InterfaceB>). If a class bound is present, it must appear first before any interface bounds.

pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 5. dry run before execution for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

checkpoint.question: What does the Java compiler replace an unbounded type parameter <T> with during bytecode type erasure?
options: java.lang.Object
java.lang.Class
void
It keeps the generic type name T in bytecode instructions
checkpoint.explanation: During compilation, Java's compiler erases type parameters to maintain backwards compatibility with pre-generics JVMs. Unbounded types <T> are erased to Object; bounded types <T extends Number> are erased to the first bound (Number).

checkpoint.question: What technique solves the compiler error when attempting to swap two elements in a List<?> list using list.set(i, list.get(j))?
options: Delegate to a private generic helper method <T> void swapHelper(List<T> list, int i, int j) to capture the wildcard
Cast List<?> to raw List
Use reflection to modify the backing array
Declare list as volatile
checkpoint.explanation: The compiler cannot determine that the type returned by list.get(j) matches the type required by list.set(i, ...). Writing a helper <T> void helper(List<T> list, int i, int j) captures the wildcard ? as concrete type T.

pages.title: 7. Independent practice
pages.content: Solve the **Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards** practice problems in increasing difficulty. For every failure, classify it as syntax, concept, state-tracing, edge-case, or design error before changing the code.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 7. independent practice for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

checkpoint.question: In the JDK method signature public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src), why is src bounded with extends and dest with super?
options: src produces elements to read (Producer Extends), while dest consumes elements to write (Consumer Super)
dest produces memory while src consumes disk space
src must be immutable while dest must be synchronized
It is an arbitrary stylistic convention with no semantic difference
checkpoint.explanation: This is the classic example of Joshua Bloch's PECS rule: src produces elements of type T that are read, so it is ? extends T. dest consumes elements of type T that are written into it, so it is ? super T.

pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 8. mastery gate for Advanced Generics: Bounds and Wildcards.

checkpoint.question: Why does Java forbid generic array creation such as new E[capacity] or new List<String>[10]?
options: Arrays are reifiable and check their component type at runtime, but generic type arguments are erased at runtime, leading to potential heap pollution
Arrays can only store primitive numeric types in Java
The JVM heap cannot allocate memory for arrays of reference types
Generic arrays would violate the single-inheritance rule
checkpoint.explanation: Because arrays enforce their element type at runtime (throwing ArrayStoreException), they must know their component type. Type erasure removes generic arguments at compile time, making new E[] impossible for the JVM to verify safely.

checkpoint.question: Under what condition is the @SafeVarargs annotation legally applied in Java?
options: Only on static methods, final instance methods, or constructors that declare a generic varargs parameter and do not perform unsafe operations like array storing
On any abstract method in an interface
On public overridden methods that return generic collections
On any class that implements Serializable
checkpoint.explanation: @SafeVarargs suppresses heap pollution warnings on methods with generic varargs (T... args). Since varargs creates an array behind the scenes, it can only be applied to non-overridable methods (static, final, or private) or constructors.

checkpoint.question: Why does the Java compiler generate synthetic bridge methods when a class extends a generic class or implements a generic interface (e.g., class MyNode extends Node<Integer>)?
options: To preserve polymorphic method overriding in bytecode after type erasure erases the parent method signature to Object
To bridge network connections between remote JVMs
To synchronize access across worker threads
To translate Java code to native C++ instructions
checkpoint.explanation: In Node<T>, the method is setData(Object). In MyNode, it is setData(Integer). Without a synthetic bridge method setData(Object) that delegates to setData(Integer), polymorphic method dispatch (invokevirtual) would fail.

checkpoint.question: What is the formal definition of a Functional Interface in Java?
options: An interface that specifies exactly one abstract method (Single Abstract Method or SAM), regardless of default or static methods
An interface that contains only static utility methods and no abstract methods
An interface marked with @FunctionalInterface that contains no methods
Any interface that extends java.lang.Runnable
checkpoint.explanation: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM). It may also contain any number of default or static methods, as well as public methods overriding java.lang.Object (such as equals).

pages.title: 1. Prerequisite check
pages.content: Before starting **Functional Interfaces and Lambdas**, recall the Java syntax and object/model concepts required for it. Write down what you already know, then identify one question you cannot yet answer confidently. The purpose of this step is to expose a missing prerequisite before new material is introduced.
pages.teachingGoal: Learner can complete 1. prerequisite check for Functional Interfaces and Lambdas.

checkpoint.question: What is the primary purpose of the @FunctionalInterface annotation in Java?
options: It informs the compiler to generate an error if the interface does not satisfy the single abstract method (SAM) contract
It compiles the interface into a high-speed C library
It makes all methods in the interface synchronized
It is mandatory; lambda expressions cannot target interfaces lacking this annotation
checkpoint.explanation: @FunctionalInterface is an informative annotation that instructs the compiler to verify that the interface has exactly one abstract method. However, any SAM interface is functionally compatible with lambdas even without this annotation.

pages.title: 2. Build the concept
pages.content: Functional Interfaces and Lambdas should be learned through a progression from terminology and mental model to tracing, implementation, and independent application. Start with the rule, then connect the rule to one small Java example. Avoid memorizing a code template before you can explain why each important line is present.

checkpoint.question: Which core functional interface from java.util.function takes an input argument of type T and returns a boolean?
options: Predicate<T> (method boolean test(T t))
Consumer<T> (method void accept(T t))
Function<T, R> (method R apply(T t))
Supplier<T> (method T get())
checkpoint.explanation: Predicate<T> represents a predicate (boolean-valued function) of one argument, evaluated via test(t).

pages.title: 3. Build a mental model

checkpoint.question: How does the JVM execute lambda expressions under the hood compared to traditional anonymous inner classes?
options: It uses the invokedynamic bytecode instruction and LambdaMetafactory to avoid generating separate .class files on disk
It generates a separate $1.class file on disk for every single lambda expression
It interprets lambda expressions via JavaScript engine reflection
It spawns a new OS daemon thread for every lambda evaluation
checkpoint.explanation: Unlike anonymous inner classes that create .class files at compile time, Java 8+ lambdas use invokedynamic bytecode instruction. The call site is linked at runtime via LambdaMetafactory, reducing classloader footprint and memory overhead.

checkpoint.question: What category of method reference is String::compareToIgnoreCase in (s1, s2) -> s1.compareToIgnoreCase(s2)?
options: Reference to an instance method of an arbitrary object of a particular type
Reference to a static method (ContainingClass::staticMethodName)
Reference to an instance method of a particular object (containingObject::instanceMethodName)
Reference to a constructor (ClassName::new)
checkpoint.explanation: When the first parameter of the lambda becomes the target of the instance method call (s1.compareToIgnoreCase(s2)), it is a reference to an instance method of an arbitrary object (String::compareToIgnoreCase).

checkpoint.question: Given int factor = 2; factor = 3; Function<Integer, Integer> mult = x -> x * factor; Why does this code fail to compile?
options: factor is mutated after declaration, so it is neither explicitly final nor effectively final, violating lambda variable capture rules
Lambdas cannot access local variables declared outside their body
Function requires two generic type arguments of different types
Integer multiplication is not permitted inside lambda expressions
checkpoint.explanation: Local variables captured by lambda expressions must be final or effectively final (their value is never modified after initialization). Reassigning factor = 3 breaks effective finality, causing a compilation error.

checkpoint.question: Given Function<Integer, Integer> f1 = x -> x + 2; Function<Integer, Integer> f2 = x -> x * 3; What is the result of f1.andThen(f2).apply(4)?
options: 18 (evaluates (4 + 2) * 3)
14 (evaluates (4 * 3) + 2)
The value 24
The value 12
checkpoint.explanation: f1.andThen(f2) first applies f1 to the input (4 + 2 = 6), and then applies f2 to that intermediate result (6 * 3 = 18). (Contrast with f1.compose(f2) which applies f2 first).

checkpoint.question: Why does Java provide IntPredicate, LongConsumer, and DoubleFunction alongside generic Predicate<Integer>, Consumer<Long>, etc.?
options: To prevent autoboxing and unboxing overhead when operating on high-throughput primitive streams
Because Java generics forbid integers greater than 100
To allow primitive interfaces to be used without importing java.util.function
Primitive functional interfaces are synchronized by default
checkpoint.explanation: Generic collections and interfaces like Predicate<Integer> require wrapping primitives in heap objects (Integer). Primitive specializations like IntPredicate take primitive int directly, eliminating garbage collection and boxing performance penalties.

checkpoint.question: Why does list.forEach(item -> writeToFile(item)) fail to compile if writeToFile throws a checked IOException?
options: Consumer.accept() does not declare any checked exceptions in its throws clause, so checked exceptions must be caught or wrapped inside the lambda
forEach can only be invoked on read-only collections
I/O operations cannot be executed inside lambda expressions
The lambda expression must be declared as public static
checkpoint.explanation: A lambda expression cannot throw checked exceptions that are not declared in the target functional interface's abstract method signature. Since Consumer.accept() declares no throws, checked exceptions must be handled (or wrapped in RuntimeException) inside the lambda.

checkpoint.question: Inside a lambda expression defined within an instance method of class Widget, what does the this keyword refer to?
options: The enclosing Widget instance (lexical scoping)
An instance of the generated lambda class
The functional interface itself
null
checkpoint.explanation: Lambdas are lexically scoped: this inside a lambda refers to the enclosing instance of the class in which the lambda is written. In contrast, this inside an anonymous inner class refers to the anonymous inner class instance itself.

checkpoint.question: What is the fundamental lifecycle of a Java Stream pipeline?
options: A data source creates the stream, zero or more lazy intermediate operations transform it, and exactly one terminal operation triggers execution and produces a result
A stream eagerly computes every element into a temporary file before returning
A stream modifies the underlying data source in-place and returns an iterator
A stream requires manual garbage collection via close() on every instance
checkpoint.explanation: Java Stream pipelines are structured into: (1) Stream source, (2) Intermediate operations (lazy, returning a new Stream), and (3) A single terminal operation (eager, executing the pipeline and consuming the stream).

checkpoint.question: How do Java Streams fundamentally differ from Java Collections?
options: Collections are in-memory data structures holding elements, whereas Streams are computation pipelines that process elements on demand without storing data
Streams can only contain primitive integers
Collections cannot be iterated more than once
Streams are mutable and allow direct index modification
checkpoint.explanation: Collections represent data at rest in memory (data structures). Streams represent data in motion (computational pipelines). Streams do not store elements and do not modify the backing collection.

checkpoint.question: What happens when the intermediate operation stream.filter(x -> x > 10) is invoked without a terminal operation?
options: Nothing executes; intermediate operations are lazy and only execute when a terminal operation is called
All elements are immediately filtered into a new ArrayList
An IllegalStateException is thrown
The stream begins background processing on worker threads
checkpoint.explanation: Intermediate operations in Java Streams are lazy: they build the pipeline description. No filtering or processing occurs until an eager terminal operation (such as collect, forEach, count, etc.) is invoked.

ConcurrentModificationException
NoSuchElementException
UnsupportedOperationException
checkpoint.explanation: Streams are single-use traversals. Once a terminal operation completes, the stream is consumed. Any further operation on that stream instance throws java.lang.IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed.

checkpoint.question: In stream processing, when should flatMap be used instead of map?

When you want to convert all elements into uppercase strings
When you need to sort elements in reverse order
When the stream contains primitive integers only
checkpoint.explanation: map applies a one-to-one transformation: T -> R. flatMap applies a one-to-many transformation: T -> Stream<R>, flattening nested streams into a single composite stream (analogous to flattening a List<List<T>> into List<T>).

checkpoint.explanation: Streams process elements on demand. findFirst is a short-circuiting terminal operation. Element 1 is tested (false), element 2 is tested (false), element 3 is tested (true) and satisfies findFirst, terminating the pipeline immediately. Thus 1 2 3 is printed.

Streams automatically roll back external mutations

partitioningBy only works with numbers

partitioningBy runs in parallel while groupingBy runs sequentially

checkpoint.question: In static double sum(List<? extends Number> list), why is <? extends Number> used instead of <Number>?

Because Java prohibits declaring methods with List<Number> parameters

4. **Lifetime:** what must be closed, awaited, copied, or released?

### Debugging Bounds, Wildcards and Variance

**Logic:** the program runs but produces an incorrect state or output.

**Concurrency / lifecycle:** the code is valid in isolation but fails because timing, ownership, cleanup, or shared state was handled incorrectly.

- **Trying to add arbitrary values to ? extends collections:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Using raw List instead of a wildcard:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Forgetting null is the only safe add to ? extends:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Choosing wildcard syntax without identifying data flow:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.

**Debugging loop:** reproduce -> isolate -> state the rule -> fix one cause -> rerun the smallest failing case.

### Stream Pipelines: map, filter, reduce

Stream Pipelines: map, filter, reduce becomes useful when Java code needs to express a stable rule rather than a one-off syntax trick. Start with the mental model: identify the values or states involved, the operation Java performs, and the contract the surrounding code expects.

**Learning focus**
- **stream source** — understand the rule and when it belongs in a production design.
- **map** — understand the rule and when it belongs in a production design.
- **filter** — understand the rule and when it belongs in a production design.
- **reduce** — understand the rule and when it belongs in a production design.
- **terminal operation** — understand the rule and when it belongs in a production design.

**Rule before API:** before choosing a class or method, state what must be true before the operation, what it produces, and what can fail. This keeps advanced Java from becoming API memorization.

codeCard.code: import java.util.*;public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){List<Integer>x=List.of(1,2,3,4);System.out.println(x.stream().filter(i->i%2==0).map(i->i*i).toList());}}

checkpoint.question: In the pipeline list.stream().filter(i -> i % 2 == 0).map(i -> i * i).toList(), in what order are elements processed?
options: Vertically / element-by-element: each even element passes through filter and then map immediately before the next element is examined
Horizontally / batch-by-batch: all elements are filtered into a full intermediate list, then that entire list is mapped
In random order depending on CPU core availability
Backwards from the last element to the first
checkpoint.explanation: Java streams execute vertically (pipelined) rather than horizontally. An element passes through all intermediate operations (filter -> map) until it reaches the terminal collector before the next element is fetched.

pages.title: API anatomy and design rules
pages.content:
### API anatomy

A production learner should know not just *what* an API call does, but what contract surrounds it. For **Stream Pipelines: map, filter, reduce**, pay attention to:

1. **Inputs and types:** what values are accepted?
2. **State:** what data is owned or shared?
3. **Failure modes:** which errors are compile-time, runtime, or domain failures?
4. **Lifetime:** what must be closed, awaited, copied, or released?
5. **Observability:** how can you prove the operation produced the correct result?

**Design rule:** prefer the narrowest abstraction that expresses the contract. Expose stable interfaces and value objects at boundaries; keep mutable implementation details private.

checkpoint.question: In stream.reduce(identity, accumulator), what critical mathematical property must the identity value satisfy?
options: For all x, accumulator.apply(identity, x) == x (the identity element must not alter any value it is combined with)
It must always equal zero
It must be greater than all elements in the stream
It must be a prime number
checkpoint.explanation: In stream reduction, identity must be an algebraic identity value for the accumulator: for addition it is 0 (0 + x = x), for multiplication it is 1 (1 * x = x), and for string concatenation it is "".

pages.content:
### Debugging Stream Pipelines: map, filter, reduce

When a program fails, classify the failure before changing code:

**Compile-time:** the type or API contract is invalid.

**Runtime:** the program reaches an operation whose preconditions are violated.

**Logic:** the program runs but produces an incorrect state or output.

**Concurrency / lifecycle:** the code is valid in isolation but fails because timing, ownership, cleanup, or shared state was handled incorrectly.

- **Reusing an already-consumed stream:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Expecting intermediate operations to execute immediately:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Using reduce when a collector is clearer:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Mutating external state inside forEach:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.

**Debugging loop:** reproduce -> isolate -> state the rule -> fix one cause -> rerun the smallest failing case.

checkpoint.question: Why is list.stream().filter(s -> s.length() > 3).sorted().findFirst() potentially much more expensive than list.stream().filter(s -> s.length() > 3).findFirst()?
options: sorted() is a stateful intermediate operation that must buffer and examine ALL matching elements before emitting any element, breaking short-circuiting
sorted() only works on parallel streams
findFirst() throws an exception when paired with sorted()
Sorting converts all string objects to character arrays
checkpoint.explanation: Most intermediate operations (like filter, map) are stateless. sorted() is a stateful operation: it cannot know the first element without buffering and comparing the entire stream, eliminating the early-termination benefit of findFirst().

checkpoint.question: What was the primary design intent of java.util.Optional<T> introduced in Java 8?

checkpoint.question: What is the critical difference between optional.orElse(computeDefault()) and optional.orElseGet(() -> computeDefault())?

checkpoint.question: In Optional<T>, what is the difference between optional.map(mapper) and optional.flatMap(mapper)?
options: If mapper returns an Optional<U>, map produces Optional<Optional<U>>, whereas flatMap flattens it into Optional<U>
flatMap converts the Optional into a List
map only works on String values
flatMap can only be invoked on empty Optionals
checkpoint.explanation: Just like in Streams, map wraps the function result in Optional.ofNullable(), causing nesting if the function itself returns an Optional. flatMap expects the mapping function to return an Optional<U> directly without adding an extra layer of wrapping.

pages.title: Debugging and failure analysis
pages.content:
### Debugging Optional and Functional Error Handling

When a program fails, classify the failure before changing code:

**Compile-time:** the type or API contract is invalid.

**Runtime:** the program reaches an operation whose preconditions are violated.

**Logic:** the program runs but produces an incorrect state or output.

**Concurrency / lifecycle:** the code is valid in isolation but fails because timing, ownership, cleanup, or shared state was handled incorrectly.

- **Calling get without checking presence:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Using Optional for every field in a domain model:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Confusing orElse with orElseGet side effects:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.
- **Returning null from a method that promises Optional:** apply the rule, isolate the smallest failing case, and verify the corrected behavior.

**Debugging loop:** reproduce -> isolate -> state the rule -> fix one cause -> rerun the smallest failing case.

checkpoint.question: Why is optional.get() without a prior optional.isPresent() considered a severe anti-pattern in modern Java code?
options: If the Optional is empty, optional.get() throws NoSuchElementException, recreating the exact same crash risk as NullPointerException
The Java compiler deprecates optional.get() with a compilation error
optional.get() triggers full garbage collection cycles
optional.get() modifies the Optional state to empty
checkpoint.explanation: Calling .get() unconditionally defeats the entire purpose of Optional. Idiomatic alternatives include .orElse(), .orElseGet(), .orElseThrow(), or functional transformations with .map() and .ifPresent().

pages.title: Mastery and interview review
pages.content:
### Mastery review

Before moving on, you should be able to explain **Optional and Functional Error Handling** without looking at code, implement the smallest correct version, identify one edge case, and justify one API-design choice.

**Mastery checklist**
- [ ] Use Optional to represent a possible absence explicitly.
- [ ] Chain map, filter, flatMap, orElse and orElseGet safely.
- [ ] Know when Optional improves an API and when it adds unnecessary complexity.

**Interview connection:** explain the feature in 30 seconds, give one runnable example, and name one failure mode or design trade-off.

**Transfer challenge:** change one requirement in the examples and predict what part of the implementation must change.

checkpoint.question: Why should Optional generally NOT be used as method parameter types or class instance fields?
options: It does not implement Serializable, increases heap memory overhead, and forces callers to wrap values unnecessarily (use overloading or nulls for parameters instead)
The JVM refuses to instantiate classes containing Optional fields
Optional fields cause severe race conditions in multi-threaded code
It causes compile-time errors in Java 11 and above
checkpoint.explanation: Optional was never intended as a general-purpose value wrapper. It is not Serializable (breaking Java serialization and frameworks like Hibernate/JPA) and creates unnecessary object allocation overhead when used as fields or method parameters.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: Optional map
codeExamples.code: import java.util.*;public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){Optional<String>x=Optional.of("java");System.out.println(x.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("NONE"));}}
codeExamples.explanation: map transforms the contained value only when present.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: Optional filter
codeExamples.code: import java.util.*;public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){Optional<Integer>x=Optional.of(8).filter(v->v%2==0);System.out.println(x.orElse(-1));}}
codeExamples.explanation: filter keeps a present value only when the predicate passes.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: ofNullable
codeExamples.code: import java.util.*;public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){String x=null;System.out.println(Optional.ofNullable(x).orElse("UNKNOWN"));}}
codeExamples.explanation: ofNullable safely converts a nullable reference into Optional.

codeExamples.label: Java
codeExamples.title: orElseGet
codeExamples.code: import java.util.*;public class Main{public static void main(String[]a){Optional<String>x=Optional.empty();System.out.println(x.orElseGet(()->"generated"));}}
codeExamples.explanation: orElseGet computes the fallback only when needed.
